paras: The attempted lynching of Howell Edmunds took place on the night of July 4, 1881, when five masked men tried to take Edmunds from the jail at Monticello, Drew County, Arkansas, where he was held on a charge of murdering his sister-in-law, Sallie Watson. Sheriff Hammock turned the men back, and Edmunds remained in jail while papers predicted that he would still be lynched. The case drew notice because the dead girl belonged to a prominent Drew County family, and the attempt was reported as far away as Chicago and Wisconsin.

Sallie Watson, described as 16 or about 17 years old, was the daughter of J. R. Watson, who lived eight miles from Monticello and was called one of the most wealthy and influential citizens of the county. She was missed on a Thursday morning, and her body was found on Saturday a few hundred yards from the house, partly covered with cut bushes and with ax wounds to the head.

Edmunds, a brother-in-law of the dead girl who was also called her cousin and the nephew and son-in-law of her father, was arrested by another brother-in-law, Stephen Gaster, and lodged in the Monticello jail. The Memphis Appeal listed the evidence said to point to him: his behavior on a fishing trip that morning, a younger sister's account of his talking with Sallie at the cow-pen, a Black woman's report that she saw him pass with a shotgun and a hand-ax, and a bloodied ax. Other reports said he had 'ruined' the girl and had offered a doctor money for an abortion; these claims came from the accusing side.

On July 4 a Monticello special to the Arkansas Gazette reported that excitement was intense and that he might be lynched that night. The next day's special said that between two and three hundred men were in town that night, but only five masked men tried to get the prisoner out of jail. The men 'seemed to be very determined', the dispatch said, but the attempt was frustrated by the 'strategy, coolness and bravery' of Sheriff Hammock. The Chicago Tribune's own dispatch said simply that the lynchers were driven away, and no one is reported hurt.

The Monticello special described indignation against the prisoner as 'intense and universal', while 'cooler heads' urged that the law take its course. As late as July 9 the Memphis Appeal expected that he would be lynched, and it reported that his wife, the dead girl's sister, had turned against him after finding a bloody shirt. No report of an arrest of the masked men, an indictment, or a trial of Edmunds appears in the coverage.

All of the coverage came from white papers, and it treated Edmunds's guilt as settled. The Memphis Appeal ran the Monticello special under the headline 'An Arkansas Fiend' and its own account under a headline calling the murder a crime for which the law did not provide adequate punishment, describing Edmunds as 'the fiend in human shape' and 'the villain'. The Chicago Tribune headed its July 6 dispatch 'Attempted Lynching' and wrote that there was 'little doubt that Judge Lynch will decide the case'; the next day it carried the Monticello special as 'A Murdered Girl'.

Short telegrams in the Cheyenne Daily Leader and the Eureka Daily Sentinel called his guilt 'certain' and said the girl's head had been cut entirely off, a detail not in the fuller Arkansas accounts. A brief that ran in the Batesville Guard and the Canton, Mississippi, American Citizen said only that the proofs were so strong that he 'narrowly escaped lynching'. A Wisconsin crime digest raised the crowd to six hundred and credited the sheriff with foiling its 'advance guard'. The first Monticello special, reporting the arrest and the fear of a lynching, was reprinted in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on July 5 and the Daily Kennebec Journal on July 6.

The size of the gathering differs: the Monticello special gave two to three hundred men in town, while the Mineral Point Tribune said six hundred gathered to lynch him. The local special is the closer source, and both versions agree that only a small party actually went at the jail.

bases: Five masked men, out of a crowd gathered in Monticello, tried to take the accused prisoner from jail to lynch him and were turned back by the sheriff, an attempted lynching (A3, A4, A7, A12).

The Tribune's own Little Rock dispatch (A3) and the Monticello special carried by the Memphis Appeal and the Tribune (A4, A7) agree that an attempt to lynch Edmunds was made and repelled, and a crime digest (A12) reports the same.

accounts.label: Monticello special via Little Rock (Arkansas Gazette)
accounts.gist: On July 4 Edmunds was in jail, excitement was intense, and a lynching was feared that night; on July 5 the special said five masked men out of two or three hundred in town tried to get him out of jail but were frustrated by Sheriff Hammock.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune special dispatch
accounts.gist: An attempt was made to lynch Edmunds; the lynchers were driven away, but feeling was so strong that 'Judge Lynch' was expected to decide the case.

accounts.label: Terrell Harris, to the Memphis Appeal
accounts.gist: A detailed case against Edmunds (behavior on the fishing trip, an ax with blood on it, a child's and a Black woman's testimony), his arrest by Gaster, and a prediction that 'infuriated citizens' would lynch him.

accounts.label: Weekly crime digest
accounts.gist: Six hundred men gathered Monday night to lynch Edmunds; the 'advance guard' was foiled by the sheriff.

framing.detail: The Monticello special headed 'An Arkansas Fiend' declared 'no doubt' of Edmunds's guilt and that the evidence would 'make him swing', while praising the sheriff who stopped the mob and the 'cooler heads' who urged legal process.
The Chicago Tribune ran the story as 'Attempted Lynching' and predicted that 'Judge Lynch will decide the case'.

The Memphis Appeal's headline called the killing a crime 'for Which the Law Does Not Provide Anything Like Adequate Punishment' and called Edmunds 'the fiend in human shape' and 'the villain' expected to be lynched.
Distant papers ran short wire items stressing that lynching was feared and that he 'narrowly escaped lynching'.

info: Night of Monday, July 4, 1881 (the July 5 dispatches refer to 'last night'; A12 says 'Monday night')
Howell Edmunds (also printed Howel Edmuns, Howard Edmonds/Edmunds, H. G. Edmunds, Howe Edmunds), a prisoner in the Monticello jail; not harmed. His race is not stated.
Charged with murdering Sallie Watson, 16 or 17, his sister-in-law, whose body was found in the woods near her father's home; papers also said he had 'ruined' or 'outraged' her
Five masked men made the attempt; two to three hundred men were reported in town that night (A4, A7), six hundred in a later digest (A12)
Attempt failed; Edmunds remained in jail with lynching still feared. No report of a trial or later fate was found.
